questions.stem: Which seven stories from The Complete Stories are set for study?
options: All seven stories in the 'Every Move You Make' section
All of the stories in the 'Dream Stuff' section
The first seven stories in the book, whatever their section
Any seven stories that each school chooses from the book
questions.explanation: VCAA sets every story in the 'Every Move You Make' section. These seven first appeared together in Malouf's 2006 collection of that name.

questions.stem: In 'The Valley of Lagoons', what is the trip the teenage narrator joins?
options: A droving trip to take cattle across the Northern Territory
A pig-shooting trip to a wetland in north Queensland
A fishing trip to the reef off the Queensland coast
A crocodile-hunting trip on a river in the Northern Territory
questions.explanation: The 'valley' is a country of lagoons and swamps rather than a true valley. The hunting trip is the narrator's first, and it works as a rite of passage into the world of men.

questions.stem: Who narrates 'The Valley of Lagoons', and from what point of view?
options: The McGowans' father, in the first person, describing his sons' first hunt
An unnamed narrator, in the third person, moving between all the hunters
Angus's older sister, in the first person, hearing about the trip afterwards
Angus, in the first person, looking back on the trip from later in life
questions.explanation: Angus tells the story himself, remembering his teenage self with an adult's understanding. This lets him show both his excitement at the time and what he only grasped later.

questions.stem: VCAA describes 'The Valley of Lagoons' as a pig hunt that highlights 'the fractures of a childhood friendship'. Why does the hunt expose these cracks?
options: One boy is injured on the trip and blames his friend for the accident
The friends are separated when one family moves away during the trip
Moving into the adult world of men tests bonds formed in childhood
The boys argue over who has the right to keep the pig they shoot
questions.explanation: On the trip the narrator meets new expectations of toughness and belonging. The hunt marks a passage from childhood to early adulthood, and not everything from childhood survives it.

questions.stem: In 'The Valley of Lagoons', why is Stuart's presence on the trip awkward for Angus?
options: Stuart owns the land where the hunt takes place
Stuart has fallen for Angus's sister, Katie
Stuart once beat Angus in a fight at their school
Stuart is Angus's English teacher at the local high school
questions.explanation: Stuart's link with Angus's sister ties the narrator's family to the hunting party in an uncomfortable way. It adds tension to a trip already full of things left unsaid.

questions.stem: In 'Every Move You Make', what happens to Mitchell, Jo's partner?
options: He goes missing at sea, and Jo waits for years for his return
He dies after an accident, and Jo sees how little she knew him
He leaves Jo for another woman, and she follows him overseas
He loses his job, and the two of them move from the city to the country
questions.explanation: Mitchell's death forces Jo to piece together who he really was. She discovers parts of his life she never knew, which raises the story's central question.

questions.stem: Malouf said that in 'Every Move You Make' the woman notes tiny domestic things, like a match or a bit of fluff. Why?
options: She wants to control him, keeping track of every move he makes
She is writing a novel and needs details for her main character
She is trying to build a picture of a man she cannot fully know
She is keeping a record so that she can leave him with evidence
questions.explanation: The small details are clues to a man who keeps much of himself hidden; she is trying to know him, not to police him. The story asks whether we can ever truly know someone, even someone we love.

questions.stem: In 'War Baby', what happens to Charlie Dowd?
options: He is conscripted to fight in Vietnam and later returns home
He refuses conscription and is sent to prison for two years
He is born during the war and never learns who his father was
He is killed in Vietnam, and his family receive his letters
questions.explanation: Charlie faces conscription for the Vietnam War, goes, and comes back. The story follows the gap between the young man who left and the man who returns.

questions.stem: Why is the story called 'War Baby'?
options: War shapes Charlie's life from the start: his father died at war, and now he is sent
Charlie's girlfriend has a baby while he is away fighting in the Vietnam War
Charlie is too immature for war, and the title mocks how childish he is
The title is ironic, since Charlie is never actually sent to the war
questions.explanation: Charlie's father also died at war, and now Charlie himself is called up and goes. The title suggests how war passes from one generation of Australian men to the next, rather than mocking Charlie.

questions.stem: What is the situation in 'Towards Midnight'?
options: An old man in Brisbane remembers the night he left home to go to war
A teenage girl in Italy sneaks out each night to meet a young swimmer from the village
A seriously ill older woman in Tuscany watches a young man swim in her pool at night
A young woman in Sydney waits up each night for her husband to come home
questions.explanation: The woman is facing her own decline in an Italian village near Siena. Watching the young workman swim gives her a vivid image of the life of the body she is losing.

questions.stem: What does the young swimmer seem to represent for the woman in 'Towards Midnight'?
options: The husband she lost, who also loved to swim in the sea when he was young
Youth, health and the life of the body, set against her illness
The danger of trusting strangers who come to work in her home
The son she never had, whom she plans to leave her house to
questions.explanation: The swimmer's strong, easy body contrasts with hers. Watching him becomes a way of facing death while still feeling connected to life.

questions.stem: In 'Elsewhere', why does Andy drive to Sydney?
options: For the funeral of his sister-in-law, with his father-in-law
For a job interview at a city mine, with his younger brother
For his own wedding, with his parents and his best friend
For a holiday by the sea, with his wife and their children
questions.explanation: Andy, a down-to-earth miner from the country, travels with his wife's father to bury the man's daughter. In the city they meet the bohemian world she had chosen.

questions.stem: What does Andy come to understand by the end of 'Elsewhere'?
options: His sister-in-law was unhappy and wished she had stayed home
Country values are better than the city's, so he is glad to go home
Any other life he longs for has to be found within himself
The city offers the freer life he wants, if only he has the courage to stay
questions.explanation: Malouf said Andy hopes the city might offer adventure and a different life. In the end he sees that the 'elsewhere' he wants is not a place, city or country, but something inside him.

questions.stem: In 'Mrs Porter and the Rock', where has Mrs Porter's son, Donald, taken her?
options: To see Uluru, which she insists on climbing to the top
To Europe, to visit the cathedrals she loves
To the beach, where she spent her childhood
To see Uluru, which she tries hard not to look at
questions.explanation: Donald brings his reluctant mother to the Rock as a treat. She resists it, and her mind keeps drifting to small memories from her own life instead.

questions.stem: What fills Mrs Porter's mind instead of the Rock?
options: Worries, such as the cost of the trip and the state of her house at home
Stories, such as the guidebook's history of the Rock that Donald reads aloud to her
Memories of her husband, her past and her childhood
Plans, such as the trip to Europe she and Donald will take next summer
questions.explanation: She is drawn back into memories of her husband, her earlier life and her childhood, while the Rock barely registers. Past and present blur together.

questions.stem: How does 'Mrs Porter and the Rock' end?
options: Mrs Porter decides to stay in the Centre for good and sends Donald home without her
Mrs Porter falls ill at the Rock and is flown home to Queensland by her son
Through visions, Mrs Porter feels joined to something larger and senses she will live forever
Donald finally persuades his mother to climb the Rock, and she enjoys the long view from the top
questions.explanation: Mrs Porter's resistance gives way to strange visions in which the Rock and her memories merge. She ends with a sense of continuity beyond her own life.

questions.stem: Who is Sam McCall in 'The Domestic Cantata'?
options: A singer who has lost his voice and cannot perform
A music teacher who lives alone with his memories
A composer living in a busy, noisy family household
A conductor who has left his family to tour the world
questions.explanation: Sam's music grows out of, and competes with, the crowded life of his family. Malouf said the story is partly about the selfishness of artists and the people who make their work possible.

questions.stem: Why is 'The Domestic Cantata' structured like a cantata?
options: It repeats a single refrain, like the chorus of a popular song
It is told by one narrator in a single scene with no dialogue
It is a series of letters written by Sam to his music students
It moves through 'movements' and many voices, like a piece of music
questions.explanation: A cantata is a musical work for several voices. Malouf said the story tries a 'whole lot of movements' and shifts between many characters' minds, so the household itself becomes a kind of music.

questions.stem: How does Malouf present Mrs Porter?
options: As a comic figure whose stubbornness is mocked rather than understood
As a stubborn, ordinary older woman whose wandering memories reveal a rich inner life
As a wealthy, well-travelled woman who looks down on her son and all of his choices
As a frail, confused woman whose memories show she has lost touch with life
questions.explanation: Malouf described her as like many Australian women who left school early and married cleverer men. Her stubbornness is comic, but it is treated with sympathy, and her drifting memories reveal an inner life that is deep and moving rather than confused.

questions.stem: In 'The Domestic Cantata', what tension does Sam McCall embody?
options: Between his love of city life and his wish to retire to a quiet farm
Between his duty to his country and his fear of being sent to war
Between his loyalty to his old friends and to his new and wealthy neighbours
Between an artist's need to create and the demands of the people around him
questions.explanation: Sam's music depends on a household that also constantly interrupts him. The story asks what an artist owes to the family that sustains him.

questions.stem: Where was David Malouf born, the state where several set stories take place?
options: Perth, Western Australia
Brisbane, Queensland
Melbourne, Victoria
Hobart, Tasmania
questions.explanation: Malouf was born in Brisbane in 1934, to a Lebanese father and an English-born mother. Queensland's landscapes and people run through his fiction.

questions.stem: Which award did Every Move You Make, the collection the seven set stories come from, win?
options: The Age Book of the Year for fiction
The Miles Franklin Award
The Stella Prize
The Booker Prize for fiction
questions.explanation: The 2006 collection won The Age Book of the Year (fiction) in 2007. The Miles Franklin is awarded to novels and the Stella to women writers. The stories were then gathered into The Complete Stories.

questions.stem: 'War Baby' draws on Australia's conscription for the Vietnam War. How were young men chosen?
options: By a ballot drawn by birth dates
By a ballot of names drawn from the electoral roll
By call-up of men in strict order of their age
By an exam that tested fitness
questions.explanation: Under National Service, 20-year-old men were called up if their birthday was drawn in a ballot, not their name. Malouf said he found a young man facing that 'lottery' a very interesting subject.

questions.stem: Malouf lived for long periods in Italy. Which set story draws on that experience?
options: The Valley of Lagoons
Towards Midnight
War Baby
Elsewhere
questions.explanation: 'Towards Midnight' is set in a village near Siena in Tuscany. Malouf often writes about Australians abroad and the idea that 'Australia is not one place'.

questions.stem: Uluru is a sacred site for its Anangu traditional owners. How does this deepen 'Mrs Porter and the Rock'?
options: Mrs Porter's visions hint at a spiritual meaning in the land that tourists miss
Donald explains the Anangu law to his mother, and she agrees to respect it
Mrs Porter meets the traditional owners, who tell her the whole story of the Rock
The story argues that the Rock should be open to everyone to climb freely
questions.explanation: For tourists the Rock is a sight to tick off. Mrs Porter, almost against her will, senses something older and sacred in it, which raises questions about how settler Australians see the land.

questions.stem: Which question is at the heart of 'Every Move You Make'?
options: Can grief be overcome by starting a new life somewhere else?
Can we ever truly know another person, even one we love?
Is it better to live in the city or out in the country?
Should young people be forced to fight in wars?
questions.explanation: Jo loves Mitchell, yet after his death she learns how much of him was hidden. Malouf shows the gaps that remain even in the closest relationships.

questions.stem: VCAA says Malouf shows that 'the silences between us' are 'the sites of our greatest grief'. Which story best shows this through war?
options: 'Elsewhere', where Andy meets his sister-in-law's friends in Sydney
'The Domestic Cantata', where Sam's large family fill the house with noise
'Towards Midnight', where the woman watches a swimmer in her pool
'War Baby', where Charlie's experience of war can never be fully shared
questions.explanation: Charlie comes home with experiences he cannot put into words, and others cannot reach them. The silence around war is one of the collection's most painful gaps.

questions.stem: How do 'The Valley of Lagoons' and 'Mrs Porter and the Rock' present the Australian landscape?
options: As a beautiful backdrop that mirrors the characters' moods
As a hostile wilderness that the characters struggle to survive
As a pleasant holiday spot best seen through a camera
As a powerful presence that changes the people who enter it
questions.explanation: The lagoons stay with Angus for life, and the Rock breaks through Mrs Porter's resistance. In Malouf, land is not a backdrop or an enemy; it shapes identity and memory.

questions.stem: What do 'Towards Midnight' and 'Mrs Porter and the Rock' share?
options: An older woman near the end of her life who finds an unexpected connection to life
A young man who leaves the country town to go and make his fortune in the big city
A family argument about who will inherit the house after a death
A soldier who returns from war unable to speak about what he saw
questions.explanation: Both women face illness, age or death, and both reach a moment of acceptance or continuity: a swimmer's body, visions at the Rock. Malouf treats ageing with tenderness and humour.

questions.stem: What contrast drives 'Elsewhere'?
options: Between Australian and Italian ways of mourning the dead
Between country life and a freer, bohemian city world
Between the dry inland and the tropical north coast
Between rich mine owners and the miners they employ
questions.explanation: Andy and his father-in-law are country men in a city where no one knows them. Malouf said he was interested in the city-country divide and the loneliness inside families.

questions.stem: VCAA notes that Malouf 'weaves Australian vernacular with rich imagery'. What is the effect?
options: Familiar places and voices are made vivid and full of meaning
The stories feel plain and documentary, without symbolic depth
The dialect marks characters as uneducated, inviting readers to judge them
The everyday speech undercuts the imagery, making it seem ironic
questions.explanation: Everyday Australian speech grounds the characters with respect rather than mockery, while rich imagery lifts ordinary places, such as a swamp or a suburban house, into something memorable. The two work together rather than against each other.

questions.stem: In 'Mrs Porter and the Rock', the narration stays close to Mrs Porter's thoughts. What does this allow?
options: We share her drifting, confused memories from the inside
We judge her from the outside as Donald's friends would
We learn the full history of the Rock in an objective way
We follow several tourists' views of the Rock in turn
questions.explanation: Staying close to Mrs Porter's mind lets past and present blur as they do for her. Readers see her stubbornness with humour, but also the depth of her inner life.

questions.stem: Critics note Malouf's skill at showing how an ordinary object can hold the past. Why does this matter in the set stories?
options: Objects work as fixed symbols, each standing for one idea across the collection
Objects show that Malouf is more interested in setting than in character
Small things carry memories and feelings that characters cannot say aloud
Expensive objects show which of the characters are rich and which are poor
questions.explanation: A match on the floor, a younger self's belongings, a remembered dolphin: objects hold what characters cannot express. Their meaning shifts with each character's memories, which suits a writer so interested in silence.

questions.stem: 'This was the country I would go on dreaming in.' What does this line from 'The Valley of Lagoons' suggest?
options: The landscape of the trip stays with the narrator for the rest of his life
The narrator plans to buy the land and build a house of his own there one day
The narrator longs to leave Queensland and dream of other places
The narrator was later haunted by nightmares about the violent hunt
questions.explanation: Looking back, Angus sees that the lagoons became part of his inner life. The line shows how a place can shape a person's imagination and identity, and its tone is one of attachment rather than horror or escape.

questions.stem: In 'War Baby', Charlie returns and finds that 'the boy was still there'. What does this suggest?
options: His younger brother has waited for him all along at the family home
His childhood has ended, and only the memory of the boy remains
He is still too young to be treated as a grown man
His younger self survives alongside the man the war has changed
questions.explanation: Charlie's younger self, with his things still in place, has not disappeared. The line captures the strange double life of someone changed by war yet still carrying who he was, rather than a clean break with childhood.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'Malouf's stories show that the deepest feelings are the ones that go unspoken.' Discuss.
options: Malouf suggests that silence, not speech, holds his characters' strongest feelings
David Malouf was born in Brisbane in 1934 and has written many novels, poems and stories
This essay will discuss feelings and silence in Malouf's The Complete Stories
In 'Every Move You Make', Jo is in a relationship with a man called Mitchell
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the prompt and sets up an argument. The others give biography, announce the essay or retell the plot.

questions.stem: A student writes: "In 'Mrs Porter and the Rock', Mrs Porter won't look at the Rock." How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Explain how her refusal shows her resisting a place that will change her
Name the technique, such as characterisation, and give the page number
Retell what happens next, when Mrs Porter has her visions at the Rock
Add a quotation that shows she refuses to look at the Rock
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what a detail suggests. Naming a technique, retelling the plot or adding a quotation without comment is still not analysis; linking her refusal to the change the Rock finally works in her connects evidence to Malouf's ideas about land and spirit.
